summary: Summarizes how hosts with more than one network interface behave in practice. It describes in detail how several common operating systems deal with the challenges, such as choosing which interface to use. This is an informational survey of current practices.

plainLanguage.summary: A phone may have wifi and cellular at once, and must pick which to use. This document records how different computers make that choice.

questions: how do multi-homed hosts choose an interface
how do mobile phones handle wifi and cellular
subtitle: How different operating systems handle devices with multiple network connections

tldr.problem: Devices increasingly have multiple network interfaces (wifi and cellular, wired and wireless) but the Internet Protocol was designed assuming a single path; hosts must choose which interface to use, configure DNS, select source addresses, and handle overlapping private address spaces.
tldr.mechanism: This document surveys real-world practices in mobile handsets (Nokia S60, Windows Mobile, Android, BlackBerry, Brew) and desktop systems (Windows, Linux, BSD), showing three broad approaches: centralized connection managers, per-application settings, and stack-level policies for DNS and routing.
tldr.outcome: There is no universal best practice. Mobile systems often use connection managers to assign applications to interfaces based on cost and availability, while desktop systems rely more on routing tables and address selection rules. The lack of consistency means multi-interface hosts often do not provide a seamless user experience.

facts.label: Common DNS approach
facts.value: Query primary interface first, fall back to others

facts.label: Consistency across platforms
facts.value: Very little for DNS and routing; more for address selection

today: RFC 6419 is an Informational document describing practices as of November 2011. It has not been obsoleted. Modern devices continue to use similar approaches, though operating systems have evolved. The lack of standardization across platforms remains a challenge for multi-interface host behavior.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
More hosts are operating in multiple-interface environments, where a device is simultaneously connected to multiple networks via different technologies. A mobile phone might use cellular data and wifi at the same time; a laptop might be connected to both wired Ethernet and wireless. This document surveys how common operating systems in real deployments handle the challenges this creates: how they choose which interface to use, configure DNS servers, select source addresses, and manage overlapping private IP address spaces.

The document covers mobile handset operating systems (Nokia S60, Microsoft Windows Mobile and Windows Phone 7, RIM BlackBerry, Google Android, Qualcomm Brew, and Leadcore Arena) and desktop operating systems (Microsoft Windows, Linux, and BSD). It is a record of what implementations actually do, not a prescription of how they should work, and documents the fact that there is no consistent approach across platforms.
sections.plainLanguage: Your phone might connect to the internet through wifi or through the cellular network, sometimes both. Different phones handle this choice in completely different ways.

sections.title: Three Broad Approaches to Multiple Interfaces
sections.content:
Implementations use three general strategies for managing multiple interfaces. Centralized connection management is common in mobile handsets: a system-level connection manager makes interface selection decisions based on application requirements, user input, and interface properties such as cost and available bandwidth. The manager often restricts selection to one interface per application, avoiding the need for complex routing decisions.

Per-application connection settings allow applications themselves to choose which interface they use or to provide abstract requirements to a connection manager. This approach gives applications control but places the burden of managing multiple interfaces on application developers.

Stack-level solutions, used mainly in desktop operating systems, handle DNS resolution, routing, and address selection through system-level configuration and routing tables, without application involvement. Desktop systems typically receive configuration from DHCP, router advertisements, or manual setup, with support for per-interface settings varying by system. When multiple sets of configuration are available, systems typically give preference to a designated "primary" interface.

There is very little commonality in how desktop systems handle multiple sets of configuration information, with notable variations even between different versions of the same operating system.
sections.plainLanguage: Some phones have a manager that tells each app which network to use. Some let apps decide. Some computers have complicated rules about which network to pick.

sections.title: Mobile Handset Operating Systems
sections.content:
Nokia S60 uses the concept of an Internet Access Point (IAP) that contains all parameters needed to open a connection: SSID for wifi, APN for cellular, or tunnel settings for VPN. Each application can be bound to an IAP, ensuring it uses the correct DNS servers and default routes for its needs. S60 3.2 added Service Network Access Points (SNAPs) that group IAPs leading to the same destination (like "Internet" or "Corporate Intranet"), allowing the operating system to select the best available IAP within a SNAP while the application specifies only the destination network.

Microsoft Windows Mobile and Windows Phone 7 use a centralized connection manager that selects connections based on destination, cost, security, bandwidth, error rate, and latency. The manager automatically opens needed connections and closes idle ones, and can fail over when connectivity is lost. Windows Phone 7 implements RFC 3484 address selection rules for dual-stack systems and allows per-interface policies to override default preferences (such as preferring wired over wireless).

RIM BlackBerry supports multiple network interfaces (wireless and wired) that can be associated with a single or multiple IP stacks. Applications can be associated with a specific interface or allowed to select based on cost and type of service. Google Android, based on Linux, can manage multiple routing tables and uses policy-based routing with packet filtering to handle complex scenarios like overlapping address spaces. Qualcomm Brew uses netpolicies that allow applications to specify desired network type, IP version, and network profile; AMSS (the connectivity platform) selects the best matching interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Mobile phones have different systems. Some bind each app to one network. Some let the network manager pick the best one available. Some let the app decide. Some use encryption-like rules to pick a network.

sections.title: Desktop Operating Systems
sections.content:
Microsoft Windows allows configuration of default routers on multiple interfaces. When multiple interfaces have the same metric, Windows Vista and later use host-to-router load sharing (RFC 4311). For address selection, Windows implements RFC 3484 for source address selection in IPv6 and, since Vista, for IPv4. Windows supports both weak and strong host models for receiving packets, and uses DNS suffixes to route different queries to different servers.

Linux and BSD offer flexible routing through multiple routing tables (beyond the standard local and main tables) and policy-based routing that considers source address, type of service, interface name, and packet marks. This allows sophisticated handling of overlapping address spaces. For address selection, both implement RFC 3484 for IPv6 and support dual-stack configurations, with administrators able to customize the sorting with configuration files like /etc/gai.conf. Incoming packets are processed according to configurable host models (weak or strong).

DNS configuration varies significantly. Windows supports per-interface DNS server lists and uses a primary interface with fallback. Linux and BSD systems typically rely on DHCP clients that may overwrite the system-wide /etc/resolv.conf with each new interface configuration, though some DHCP clients and distributions offer per-interface options and mechanisms to prevent overwrites. Most configurable systems default to using the last-configured interface as primary unless manually designated otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: Windows computers use simple rules: pick the fastest network, or the first one. Linux and BSD computers have powerful but complicated routing rules. All of them struggle with DNS when multiple networks are available.

sections.title: Common Challenges and Lessons
sections.content:
The survey reveals fundamental challenges that current systems address in incompatible ways. DNS resolution is problematic: with multiple DNS server lists, systems must decide which to query, often giving preference to the primary interface with fallback to others. Some systems support per-interface DNS lists; others only support a single system-wide list.

First-hop selection (choosing which interface to route through) uses different mechanisms: some systems use routing metrics, others prefer statically configured defaults or the primary interface. Few systems allow configuration of different default router lists per interface.

Address selection (choosing which local IP address to use for outgoing packets) is more consistent due to RFC 3484, but many systems do not allow users to update the default policy, and there is no standard way to do so across platforms.

Overlapping address spaces (where different interfaces have private addresses in the same range) are handled variously: some systems keep interfaces completely separate; others use routing tables and interface binding. Most systems do not provide a satisfactory user experience in multi-interface environments.
sections.plainLanguage: No two systems solve these problems the same way. Should the computer ask the first DNS server or the newest one? Should it send through the fastest interface or the most reliable? There is no agreed answer.
